```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", error = FALSE)
old_options <- options(width = 90L)
old_logfile <- loggit2::get_logfile()
old_level <- loggit2::set_log_level("DEBUG", confirm = FALSE)
old_calls <- loggit2::set_call_options(confirm = FALSE)
```

`loggit2` adds structured logging to R without additional R runtime dependencies.
You can start with a single call; there is no logger object or configuration file
to create.

## Pick your starting point

| Your use case | Smallest change |
| --- | --- |
| Log messages, warnings and errors from existing code | Wrap its call in `loggit2::with_loggit()` |
| Record an event with a run ID or other context | Call `loggit2::loggit()` |
| Add logging where your own code signals a condition | Use `loggit2::message()`, `warning()`, `stop()` or `stopifnot()` |

No setup is required. By default, `get_logfile()` identifies a file in R's
temporary directory, and each entry is also echoed as JSON to stdout. For the
examples below, we choose a separate temporary file and disable that extra output.

```{r choose-file}
logfile <- tempfile(fileext = ".ndjson")
```

For a persistent log, use a path in an existing directory instead.

## Log a function you already have

Suppose this function belongs to an existing script or another package:

```{r existing-function}
import_data <- function() {
  base::message("Reading input")
  120L
}
```

Wrap its call. Nothing inside the function needs to change:

```{r capture-function}
rows <- loggit2::with_loggit(import_data(), logfile = logfile, echo = FALSE)
rows
```

The message is still displayed, the return value is still `120L`, and the
message has also been logged. Warnings and errors retain their normal behavior
too; logging does not turn an error into a successful result.

## Add context to an event

Use `loggit()` when you want to record an event without signaling a condition:

```{r record-event}
loggit2::loggit(
  "INFO", "Import completed",
  run_id = "demo-001", rows = rows,
  logfile = logfile, echo = FALSE
)
```

Named scalar fields such as `run_id` and `rows` become columns when you read the
log. Non-missing values are stored as strings, and `NA` becomes JSON `null`.

## Read the result

```{r read-events}
events <- loggit2::read_logs(logfile)
events[c("log_lvl", "log_msg", "run_id", "rows")]
```

Each row represents an event. Fields that were not supplied for an event are
`NA`. The file itself is newline-delimited JSON: one JSON object per line.

## Log conditions in your own code

The condition wrappers use the session's default log file. Select it explicitly
when you want these calls to join the same log:

```{r own-conditions}
previous_logfile <- loggit2::set_logfile(logfile, confirm = FALSE)
loggit2::message("Ready for the next input", echo = FALSE)
loggit2::set_logfile(previous_logfile, confirm = FALSE, create = FALSE)
```

`loggit2::warning()`, `stop()` and `stopifnot()` likewise log their condition and
retain the corresponding Base R behavior. `echo = FALSE` only switches off the
additional JSON output; it does not silence the condition.

Attaching `library(loggit2)` masks the corresponding Base R names for ordinary
calls. Use explicit `loggit2::` calls when you want the choice to be clear.
To capture code in another package, use `with_loggit()`.

```{r cleanup, include = FALSE}
loggit2::set_logfile(old_logfile, confirm = FALSE, create = FALSE)
loggit2::set_log_level(old_level, confirm = FALSE)
loggit2::set_call_options(.arg_list = old_calls, confirm = FALSE)
options(old_options)
unlink(logfile)
```
